title: Fitch thumbs up for Budget  | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 19 November 2026 06:38
-     - 279

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake delivering the 2027 Budget speech in Parliament last week (12)

Fitch Ratings yesterday gave Budget 2027 a major vote of confidence, saying it signals the Government’s ongoing commitment to fiscal discipline and debt reduction while accommodating higher spending on investment and cyclone reconstruction.

For a country that long grappled with twin deficits, a primary surplus and falling debt are no small gain, and coming as Parliament debates Budget 2027, Fitch’s assessment gives investors and lenders an independent signal that the hard-won adjustment of the past few years is working, even though the road ahead is long and painful trade-offs remain 

“Fiscal discipline, demonstrated again by the outperformance of fiscal targets in 2026, and a focus on debt reduction were key factors behind our upgrade of the sovereign rating to ‘B-‌’/Stable from ‘CCC+’ in September,” the rating agency said in a statement yesterday.

It noted the Budget targets a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP, down from an estimated 3.6% in 2026. “The 2026 surplus is well above the 2.5% target in last year’s budget and our earlier 2.6% forecast, reflecting stronger revenue. The decline in the surplus in 2027 reflects lower revenue and higher capital spending but remains consistent with a debt reduction path. This implies a 2027 deficit of 4.5% of GDP, wider than the 3.7% in 2026,” Fitch said.

It noted that the Budget assumptions appear credible and broadly align with Fitch Ratings’ forecasts from its September sovereign review. “The 2027 primary-surplus target is slightly below our 2.8% forecast because planned spending is higher than we assumed. However, we think there is potential for further under-execution on capex again this year, which could drive a slightly higher surplus”.

Primary expenditure is budgeted at 13.6% of GDP in 2027, above the 13% statutory ceiling under the 2024 Public Finance Management Act (PFMA). The temporary deviation from the PFMA mainly reflects capital spending for reconstruction following Cyclone Ditwah, as well as higher public capex plans. The plans include Rs. 260 billion carried forward from a supplementary budget for cyclone reconstruction passed in December 2025 but not spent in 2026 as a result of under-execution. 

“This is the second year the Government has sought a deviation from the PFMA, although budget under-execution meant the ceiling was not actually breached in 2026,” Fitch noted.

The ratings agency said sustaining recent revenue gains will help underpin strong primary surpluses. Revenue is budgeted to moderate to 15.8% of GDP in 2027 from 16.6% in 2026 and 16.7% in 2025, as the boost to import-duty collections from pent-up vehicle-import demand fades as imports normalise. However, efforts to broaden the tax base and improve compliance are supporting more broad-based revenue improvements.

“The budget is broadly aligned with International Monetary Fund program parameters. This should support the seventh review of Sri Lanka’s Extended Fund Facility. The current program ends in March 2027, and the Government announced the establishment of a committee to assess a potential follow-on arrangement, which could provide a further policy anchor,” Fitch said.

Sustained efforts to cement revenue gains and expenditure restraint will remain central to achieving ongoing debt reduction and for the future path of the sovereign rating. Over the medium term, the Government aims to maintain a primary surplus of 3.0% of GDP, requiring politically difficult trade-offs to comply with the 13% expenditure ceiling under the PFMA. Efforts to boost investment spending could help lift potential GDP growth, which we forecast at 4.2%, and support steady fiscal outcomes. However, this will depend on capex execution, effective targeting and progress on broader structural reforms.

Fitch warns fiscal vulnerabilities remain high despite the substantial fiscal adjustment achieved in the past few years. 

“We forecast Government debt will drop to about 92% of GDP in 2026, from 115% in 2022, but well above the 55% median for ‘B’ rated sovereigns. We expect interest payments to decline to around 41.0% of revenue in 2026 from nearly 80% in 2023, but remain more than three times the 12.7% ‘B’ median. A lengthening record of fiscal policy credibility and healthy primary surpluses will likely be critical towards ensuring debt sustainability and supporting potential future rating momentum,” Fitch observed.

title: Govt. puts private sector at heart of tourism growth strategy | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 19 November 2026 06:53
-     - 104

Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath – Pic by Ruwan Walpola

By Charumini de Silva

Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath positioned private sector investment and enterprise at the centre of Sri Lanka’s tourism growth strategy, acknowledging that businesses must remain its principal driving force. 

Addressing the 61st Annual General Meeting (AGM) of The Hotels Association of Sri Lanka (THASL), he said the Government’s responsibility was to create an enabling policy environment, regulate the industry and facilitate investment, while recognising the substantial contribution and risks undertaken by private operators, particularly the hoteliers. 

Govt. puts...

“If there is no private sector, there is no tourism sector; and that is the truth,” he said. 

Stressing that the industry cannot be developed through Government intervention alone, the Minister assured industry stakeholders that the private sector participation in policymaking and strategic decisions would not be curtailed. 

He stressed that developing Sri Lanka’s competitiveness would require close collaboration with businesses across international destination marketing, regional digital campaigns and infrastructure development and policy formulation. “The Government is committed to maintaining that partnership rather than attempting to develop the industry through public sector efforts alone,” 

In this context, Herath reiterated the Government’s decision announced in the 2027 Budget, to abolish the 1% Tourism Development Levy (TDL) imposed on the turnover of tourism establishments from 1 April 2027, as part of efforts to reduce the industry’s tax burden and improve competitiveness.

He explained the move would have an estimated Rs. 2.5 billion in revenue impact, but the Treasury had agreed to increase the share of the passenger embarkation levy allocated to the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) from $ 5 to $ 7.50, ensuring that funding for tourism promotion and global marketing would not be compromised. 

However, he said the separate 1% levy payable to provincial councils and municipal councils would remain, given their responsibilities for services such as waste management and other local infrastructure supporting tourism establishments. 

The Minister also highlighted the need to widen investment opportunities, particularly for SMEs and new entrants. “We need to attract more hotel developments to serve high-end travellers,” he added. 

Acknowledging the disruptions caused by Cyclone Ditwah and the Middle East conflict, Herath said, such unforeseen short term challenges would not alter the Government’s long term ambition to make the tourism industry a major contributor to the economic development. 

The Minister called on the industry stakeholders to work with the Government towards building a stronger and more sustainable tourism sector. “Together we can build a strong industry and an economy,” he said.

title: THASL Chief says $ 10 b target needs urgent reforms | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 19 November 2026 06:50
-     - 98

THASL President Asoka Hettigoda – Pic by Ruwan Walpola

Sri Lanka’s $ 10 billion tourism earnings target for 2030 remains within reach only with decisive Government action, Hotels Association of Sri Lanka (THASL) President Asoka Hettigoda said, pointing to global marketing, informal sector regulation and air connectivity as the priorities.

Addressing the Association’s 61st Annual General Meeting (AGM) on Tuesday, he said the industry remains committed to the 2030 target despite mounting external pressure from the Middle East conflict, rising airfares, higher travel insurance costs and global inflation.

Hettigoda, who was reelected to the second term, stressed that Sri Lanka could not afford to fall behind regional competitors that were investing heavily in destination marketing, insisting on an immediate and adequately funded global marketing campaign as a priority.

“We must launch a comprehensive global marketing campaign without further delay and double the current promotional allocation from Rs. 5 billion to Rs. 10 billion,” he added. 

He outlined formalising and bringing in 50,000 rooms operating outside the supervision of the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) as another critical priority. 

“This is essential to ensure fair competition, maintain quality and safety standards, and minimise foreign exchange leakages. Our objective is not to discourage small operators, but to create a fair and professionally regulated industry that benefits everyone,” he explained.

He also said the industry has called for a major improvement in international and domestic air connectivity, proposing measures to attract an additional 20 to 30 airlines and services by making Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA) more competitive in ground handling charges, aviation fuel and catering costs. Greater direct connectivity and domestic aviation links were also identified as essential to strengthening Sri Lanka’s destination appeal.

Noting that existing hotel infrastructure required substantial refurbishment and modernisation to meet the expectations of higher-spending international travellers, he called for affordable, long-term financing facilities to support reinvestment and improve service standards.

He also outlined opportunities to diversify tourism offerings through a world-class cruise terminal, wellness and Ayurveda tourism, heritage attractions and nature-based experiences, while proposing special credit facilities and concessional import tariffs for hotels that channel foreign exchange earnings through the formal banking system and reinvest them locally.

Hettigoda also welcomed the Budget’s bold infrastructure push, praising the capital allocations for aviation, ports and regional attractions as foundational investments in positioning Sri Lanka as a premier global destination. He also thanked the President for abolishing the 1% TDL to ease the heavy tax burden, stakeholders reiterated that their longstanding request was for relief from local government and municipal taxes, and urged policymakers to revisit operational, tax and regulatory concerns to sustain the sector’s growth.

However, he said to encourage broader participation from local entrepreneurs, stakeholders recommended reducing the minimum investment threshold for the 200% enhanced capital allowance from $ 3 million to $ 500,000, enabling SMEs to enter and scale within the tourism market.

Stating sustainability as a competitive advantage, he called for incentives for hotels investing in renewable energy, efficient water management and responsible waste disposal, setting an ambition for Sri Lanka to rank among the world’s top five sustainable tourism destinations within five years.

As he begins his second term as THASL President, Hettigoda said the Association’s members collectively represent over $ 15 billion in investment, more than 200 hotel-owning companies and over 20,000 rooms, underscoring the private sector’s substantial stake in the country’s tourism industry.

THASL President said achieving the country’s longer-term tourism ambitions would require decisive policy reforms, strategic investment, effective marketing and stronger collaboration between Government and industry, with success measured not merely by visitor numbers but by economic value, employment and the livelihoods generated across the country.

The SLT Group reported consolidated Profit After Tax (PAT) of Rs. 10.3 billion for the nine months ended 30 September, 2026, up 59.4% from Rs. 6.5 billion in the same period of 2025. We firmly believe that this balanced, multi-stakeholder approach is what makes our growth sustainable and our company truly a national champion.”

SLT PLC’s revenue grew to Rs. 59.9 billion, 11.0% for the nine months. Operating profit rose to Rs. 9.9 billion, 36.1%, PBT gained 35.5% and PAT grew to Rs. 6.4 billion, 58.0% from Rs. 4.1 billion, due to cost saving initiatives and efficient tax planning.

Mobitel’s revenue grew to Rs. 40.7 billion, 15.5%, higher than the Group and SLT PLC. The Operating profit rose to Rs. 5 billion, 47.2% and PBT rose to Rs. 4 billion, 76.0%. Mobitel’s PAT more than doubled, rising to Rs. 3.5 billion or 110.8%.

Group revenue for the third quarter grew to Rs. 32.7 billion, a 10.9%, an increase of Rs. 3.2 billion, direct costs rose 8.8%. Operating profit grew to Rs. 5.3 billion, 25.8% and EBITDA improved by 9.3%. Interest income from excess cash also rose to Rs. 458 million, PBT rose to Rs. 4.5 billion, 17.1%, and Group PAT grew to Rs. 3.7 billion, 69.3% increase from Rs. 2.2 billion in 3Q 2025.

At SLT PLC, 3Q revenue grew to Rs. 20.6 billion, a 11.7% growth, operating profit rose to Rs. 3.2 billion, 29.0% growth and PAT grew to Rs. 1.8 billion, a growth of 26.5%. Mobitel’s revenue climbed to Rs. 14.5 billion, 20.6%. EBITDA grew to Rs. 5.5 billion, 31%, operating profit nearly doubled, up Rs. 2.4 billion, 92.8% and PAT rose Rs. 1.8 billion, 195.5%.

Mobitel has deployed the majority of the planned 5G roll out for the year, and will proceed to expand its 5G network further, and the Group continues working on cost-saving initiatives.

In addition to infrastructure, SLT-Mobitel is actively championing Sri Lanka’s digital transformation and nation-building through next-generation technologies. Hosting national-level demonstrations of 5G and artificial intelligence, including the flagship National AI Expo, the Group is bringing immersive technology experiences to businesses, students, and citizens throughout the country.

SLT-Mobitel CEO Riyaaz Rasheed added: “The financial momentum in the first nine months of 2026 was driven by sustained demand for broadband and enterprise services, and accelerated growth at Mobitel in revenue and subscriber market share. We continue to expand our 5G footprint and FTTH rollouts, while maintaining a focus on operational efficiencies. 

“The Group’s continued focus on strengthening its financial position is reflected in its National Long-Term Rating upgrade to ‘AA+(lka)’ with a Stable Outlook, by Fitch Ratings on 4 November, 2026. We also remain aligned with the Government’s ambitions for the growth of Sri Lanka’s digital economy, providing customers and businesses with the digital infrastructure they need to grow.”

title: Banks’ appetite to lend cools as loan demand rises: CBSL survey | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 19 November 2026 06:42
-     - 181

Sri Lanka’s banks became markedly more cautious about lending in the third quarter even as demand for loans picked up, the Central Bank’s latest Credit Supply Survey showed. Their outlook for the final quarter points to a wider gap between the two. The survey comes ahead of the Central Bank’s monetary policy announcement this Friday (20).

The survey covers all licensed commercial and specialised banks. It is built on diffusion indices, which run from -100 to 100 and are weighted by each bank’s share of the sector’s total loan book. A positive reading means an increase, and the size of the number shows how widespread the change is.

Overall willingness to lend fell to 27.4 in the third quarter from 40.4 in the second. The reading is still positive, so willingness rose, but at a much slower pace. The slowdown showed up in retail (38.0 from 52.0), corporate (41.4 from 43.9) and SME lending (25.3 from 27.8).

“This overall slowdown could largely be attributed to the gradual transmission of the monetary policy tightening measures introduced in May 2026, coupled with more selective risk appetite of the banks, and regulatory and exposure limitations related constraints,” the Central Bank said.

Demand moved the other way. The demand-for-loans index rose to 42.8 from 35.1, with increases across all four sectors. This puts the demand index ahead of the willingness index for the first time since the first quarter, after willingness (40.4) had led demand (35.1) in the second.

The fourth-quarter outlook widens that gap. Willingness to lend is expected at 10.4, the lowest of the five quarters the survey covers, against expected demand of 35.1.

Corporate lending shows the widest split. Expected corporate demand rises to 52.2, while willingness to lend to corporates falls to 8.6 from 41.4. Willingness to lend to state-owned enterprises (SOEs) dropped to -78.7 in the third quarter from 1.4 in the second. The outlook for SOEs is -54.7, even as expected SOE demand, at 64.8, is the highest of any sector. Official data show credit to public corporations and State-Owned Business Enterprises fell by Rs. 16.9 billion to Rs. 462.9 billion in September, with the year-on-year contraction widening to 24% from 22.3% in August. 

“This slowdown is largely attributable to the anticipated inflationary pressures, rising operating costs, and restrictions on leasing facilities,” the Central Bank said of banks’ fourth-quarter outlook on willingness to lend.

Banks expect loan demand to keep rising in all four sectors in the fourth quarter. In retail, though, the demand index is expected to fall to 13.9 from 50.0, so retail demand will rise far less widely than before.

“The anticipated increase is primarily attributable to higher import financing requirements, seasonal demand, increased working capital needs to manage higher operating costs associated with inflationary pressures, and the expected improvement in overall economic activities,” the survey said.

Asset quality improved. The non-performing loan (NPL) index fell to -30.1 from -3.8, with NPLs declining in all four sectors, reversing the second-quarter rise in the corporate, SME and SOE sectors. The Central Bank credited accelerated recovery actions and remedial options, improved portfolio performance, and rescheduling resulting in stage upgrades. Loan rejections fell to -11.7 from -0.3. The decline came in the retail, corporate and SME sectors, while SOE rejections were broadly unchanged.

The findings fit other recent signs that credit growth is cooling. Year-on-year private credit growth slowed for a third straight month to 23.6% in September, from 24.5% in August and 26.4% in July. The banking sector’s credit-to-deposit ratio rose above 70% for the first time in three years, reaching 74.0% at end-June 2026. The Central Bank raised the Overnight Policy Rate by 100 basis points to 8.75% on 26 May, 2026. 

For Friday’s decision, the survey points both ways. The Central Bank links the slowdown in banks’ willingness to lend to the May tightening. At the same time, banks expect inflationary pressures and higher import financing needs to drive loan demand in the fourth quarter.

title: Sri Lanka’s young people most optimistic in world: Oxford Scholastica Academy study | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 19 November 2026 07:12
-     - 116

A new global survey of young people has ranked youth optimism about the future across 100 countries, with students from 41 countries providing sufficient responses, measuring how hopeful students feel about their personal futures, the economy, the environment, politics, and the future of society as a whole. 

The study by Oxford summer school provider, Oxford Scholastica Academy, received responses from 1,433 students to discover where Gen Z are the most and least optimistic about their future.

Sri Lankan students are the most optimistic in the world, scoring 4.32 out of 5 overall, while young people in Kuwait are the least hopeful, with an overall score of just 2.92.

Sri Lanka leads the study with young people reporting the highest rates of optimism, with the highest environmental optimism score of any country in the study (4.62) and strong personal optimism (4.75). Despite significant economic turbulence in recent years, Sri Lankan students remain deeply hopeful about the future of their society (4.25).

The second most optimistic country is Kenya, with students surveyed scoring 4.31 overall. Kenyan students marked feeling optimistic about the future of society (4.43, joint highest in the study alongside Cyprus) and record the highest political optimism of any country surveyed (3.96).

Nepal achieves a perfect personal optimism score of 5.00 – the only country to do so and ranked third overall. Nepal also has the highest economic optimism (4.80), suggesting that despite its lower-income status, students feel strongly positive about their individual prospects.

Kazakhstan is the fourth most optimistic nation according to the students polled, students report high economic confidence (4.56) along with the third-highest political optimism in the study (3.76).

Indonesia scores 4.07 while Nigeria scores 4.08, with Nigerian students scoring highly for environmental optimism (3.92) and Indonesian students reporting economic confidence (4.41).

Among Western nations, Canada ranks highest at sixth (4.08), comfortably ahead of the US (3.99), the UK (3.61), Germany (3.73), and France (3.22).

Oxford Scholastica Academy Co-Director Lavinia Abell said: “In every aspect of society, there are things to be anxious and pessimistic about. This could be the rise in Artificial Intelligence (AI), war, the cost-of-living increasing, and much more. This will be especially worrisome for young people, facing challenges as they enter the world of work. What this study highlights is the attitudes of each nationality towards these uncertainties. What is particularly striking is how low Italy’s political optimism scores are compared to other European nations. Even France and Poland, which also rank near the bottom, show slightly different patterns.”

The project, which works with diaspora professionals to strengthen women-led enterprises in Northern Sri Lanka through mentorship, skills development and improved access to international markets, demonstrates how diaspora expertise and investment can support entrepreneurship and regional economic development.

Ottawa: Trade development and institutional engagements

The delegation also met with officials of the High Commission of Sri Lanka in Ottawa, including Minister Counsellor Kiritharan Kumarasamy, during its visit to the mission. The program also included a visit to the Senate of Canada, organised by the High Commission of Sri Lanka, providing the delegation with an opportunity to observe Canada's parliamentary proceedings and learn more about its legislative system.

The delegation met with Global Affairs Canada Executive Director for Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Maldives Yannick Lamonde, and Trade Facilitation Office (TFO) Canada Executive Director Steve Tipman. Discussions focused on trade development and capacity building, including strengthening Sri Lankan exporters' readiness, improving access to Canadian market information and understanding market requirements and compliance standards.

Montréal: Business networking and tourism promotion

In Montréal, the delegation attended a business networking session organised by Sri Lanka's Honorary Consul in Montréal Chanaka Kurera, which was attended by local businesses, business chambers, consular representatives and other Canadian stakeholders, including representatives from the City of St-Laurent, to build business relationships and explore trade, investment and collaboration opportunities between Sri Lanka and Montréal.

The Montréal leg of the mission coincided with Sri Lanka's participation in the International Tourism & Travel Show (SITV), held from 30 October to 1 November, 2026. During the exhibition, the CanCham Sri Lanka leadership met with Tourism Deputy Minister Prof. Ruwan Ranasinghe.

The CanCham team presented the Deputy Minister with a copy of its Tourism Plan, together with the Five-Year Action Plan, which outlined the proposed priorities for its tourism sector, and further briefed him on the proposed Global Health and Wellness Summit Sri Lanka 2027 (GHWSSL) and its potential to support the development of Sri Lanka as a health and wellness tourism destination.

As a follow-up to the mission, discussions are underway to organise an inward business delegation from Canada to Sri Lanka. The proposed visit would provide Canadian investors, prospective buyers, manufacturers and tourism stakeholders with an opportunity to experience Sri Lanka's business and investment landscape first-hand, explore potential partnerships and gain a better understanding of opportunities across key sectors. The mission has also opened avenues for continued engagement, with CanCham Sri Lanka receiving invitations to participate in future business and industry events in Canada.

Across Canada, the mission covered investment and partnership opportunities in real estate, education, tourism, healthcare and wellness, agriculture and AgriTech, research and development, green housing, and financial services. Through this mission, CanCham Sri Lanka continued its efforts to position Sri Lanka as a gateway to the Indo-Pacific region, connecting Canadian expertise, investment and business networks with local opportunities while strengthening bilateral trade, investment and private-sector partnerships.

title: Economists to focus on knowledge economy as Sri Lanka grapples with eroding return on capital | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 19 November 2026 07:05
-     - 88

SLEA President Prof. Sirimevan Colombage (second from left) addresses the media briefing of the SLEA Annual International Conference 2026 in Colombo, accompanied by (from left) Vice President Dr. B. L. J. S. Balasooriya, Immediate Past President Prof. Ven. W. Wimalaratana Thero and General Secretary Nihal Rodrigo - Pic by Ruwan Walpola

As Sri Lanka grapples with eroding returns on capital, with the investment needed to generate Rs. 1 of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) doubling since 1960, the Sri Lanka Economic Association (SLEA) will hold its Annual International Conference on 21 November under the theme “Paving the Way for Sri Lanka’s Knowledge Economy”, SLEA President Prof. Sirimevan Colombage said yesterday.

“In 1960, if we invested Rs. 3, we could increase our GDP by Rs. 1. In 2025, we have to invest Rs. 6. That means we have to invest more and more to increase income,” Prof. Colombage said, citing the incremental capital output ratio (ICOR), which measures how much investment is needed to generate an additional unit of output. Declining returns on capital were the reason the country must shift to a knowledge economy, he said.

The conference, organised by the SLEA in collaboration with the Gamani Corea Foundation, will be held at the Bandaranaike Memorial International Conference Hall (BMICH) in Colombo. It will bring together local and international economists, policymakers and practitioners to discuss knowledge-driven growth strategies as the country prepares to resume external debt repayments in 2028, following economic stabilisation under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) framework in the wake of the 2022 sovereign debt default.

Prof. Colombage said Sri Lanka’s per capita income was almost on par with Singapore’s in 1960. Today, Singapore’s is nearly $ 100,000, against Sri Lanka’s about $ 5,000.

“Other countries have rapidly developed and achieved upper middle-income and high-income levels. But Sri Lanka is trapped in the lower middle-income range,” he said.

Average growth since 1978 has been around 3.5% to 4%, against more than 8% in fast-growing economies, he said. Sri Lanka achieved 8% growth on only two occasions: after economic liberalisation in 1978 and after the end of the war in 2009. Growth is expected at around 3% to 4% this year, and Central Bank and IMF projections put it at only about 3% over the next three years. Around 22% of the population lives below the poverty line, while the migration of young people is causing a loss of human capital.

Export-led growth, the objective of liberalisation, has not materialised, Prof. Colombage said. Exports as a share of GDP fell from around 26% in 1960 to 14% in 2025. In 1960, exports were sufficient to finance 90% of imports, but by 2025 they covered only 68%.

“We have become more and more inward-oriented rather than outward-oriented,” he said.

Garments still account for nearly 50% of manufactured exports, even as countries such as Vietnam and Bangladesh have opened up their economies. High-tech exports such as microchips and electronics make up only about 1.7% of Sri Lanka’s manufactured exports, against about 30% in South Korea.

“Our export industry is very much basic, I am rather disappointed to say,” Prof. Colombage said.

Citing the World Bank’s 2024 ‘3-I’ strategy, under which a country must pass through investment, infusion and innovation phases to reach high-income status, he said Sri Lanka remained stuck in the investment phase. It had failed to attract the Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and global production sharing needed to bring in technology from abroad.

“We are rather allergic to foreign direct investment,” he said.

The innovation phase requires heavy investment in research and development and education, but Sri Lanka spends less than 2% of GDP on education, and expectations of raising it to 6% have not materialised, he said.

Prof. Colombage acknowledged that Sri Lanka has fairly strong science and technology institutions, including the National Science Foundation and the National Science and Technology Commission. He pointed to a recent Budget proposal to amalgamate science and technology institutions under one umbrella, as well as digitalisation initiatives.

“Successive governments have not completely neglected this. But we need an aggressive policy framework aimed at promoting science and technology. So far, no government has produced that kind of framework,” he said.

The SLEA, established in 1985 and incorporated by an Act of Parliament in 2011, has more than 900 active members. Since February, it has held two public economic forums and six stakeholder seminars with the Gamani Corea Foundation.

For The international conference, Prof. Colombage said the SLEA chose knowledge economy as a cross-cutting theme spanning agriculture, industry and services, after recent annual sessions focused on each sector.

At the inaugural session, Prof. Colombage will deliver the Welcome and Presidential Address, and Gamani Corea Foundation Honorary Chairman Dr. Harsha Aturupane will deliver the Keynote Address. Australian National University Prof. Premachandra Athukorala will attend as Guest of Honour, and Central Bank Senior Deputy Governor Dr. Chandranath Amarasekara as Chief Guest. Prof. Athukorala’s book ‘Global Production Sharing and Trade Patterns’ will be launched at the session.

Six parallel academic sessions will follow, exploring digital infrastructure, human capital and the labour market, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), green knowledge systems, institutional governance and intellectual property.

title: Debate behind Budget debate | Daily FT

Thursday, 19 November 2026 05:23

Sajith’s Budget speech reflects concern for the underprivileged

Resting on the legacy of stellar economic achievement of paternal Presidents, Sajith and Namal are scornful of the Government’s mediocre performance and exude confidence that each could revive rapid development. Sajith’s discourse is more social-democratic and pluralist, parsing Buddhist scripture to present its rational core; Namal’s is more hard-charging, bearing a nationalist religio-cultural sub-text. Voters will have two credible options for change

This year’s Budget debate is different. Prime Minister Harini Amarasuriya spotted the change in the Opposition’s ‘batting order’.

‘…“Usually, Opposition MP Harsha de Silva opens the Budget debate on behalf of the Opposition. This has been the practice since I entered Parliament in 2020. We generally prepare ourselves to respond to his remarks. Whether we are in the Government or the Opposition, we have always been ready to listen to his opening statement following a Budget presentation. However, we see a change in that practice today,” she said…’

(https://www.newswire.lk/7xf1)

The PM followed up with a query.

‘…The Prime Minister said the Government…remained keen to hear MP Harsha de Silva’s views on the 2027 Budget.

She said his remarks would help determine whether there had been a shift in the SJB’s economic policies or whether the party continued to maintain its previous position.

Referring to the remarks made by Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa at the beginning of the debate, the Prime Minister accused him of presenting misleading narratives concerning the economy, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.

She said the Government was now awaiting MP Harsha de Silva’s contribution to establish whether other SJB parliamentarians shared the Opposition Leader’s position on these economic matters.’ (Ibid)

Namal stays cool under pressure

In a sense, her observation was misleading. The Budget having been presented by President and ruling party leader Anura Kumara Dissanayake, the global practice would be for his counterpart, the Leader of the Opposition and the largest single Opposition party, to open on behalf of the alternative Government. That’s Sajith Premadasa, not Dr Harsha de Silva. It was an anomaly, absurdly and counter-productively resorted to by the SJB since 2020, to permit the latter to open the debate for the Opposition. Sajith opening this time was a correction of that deviation—though Harsha stridently complained in his speech during this debate that “my speech was delayed by three days”.

Most revealing is the PM’s question as to “a shift in the SJB’s economic policies” (from Harsha’s?) and whether the SJB parliamentarians “shared the Opposition Leader’s position on these economic matters”.

What would the NPP Government prefer—that the SJB does or doesn’t share its leader’s position on economic matters?

Sajith’s speech showed consistency in his long-standing rejection of ‘trickle-down’ in favour of balancing ‘growth with equity’ articulated during Budget debates going back 15 years. Furthermore, he has been advocating ‘social democracy’ in Parliament since November 2022. Sajith’s speech this time was a more full-blooded elaboration of his basic economic doctrine and critique of Government policy. By opening for his side, the SJB leader signalled that his progressive-centrist economics would be the banner under which he would campaign—and run—against the Government.

The surreal irony of Harini’s question regarding SJB economic ideology was that all the speeches on the Government side including her own, reflect the degeneration of JVP-NPP economic ideology to a monolithic, dogmatic defence of liberal economic orthodoxy under the rubric of ‘stabilisation’ and ‘transformation’.

If the JVP leadership retained a residue of a Marxist critique of capitalist economics, and the NPP the slightest trace of progressive economic thinking (Stiglitz-Krugman-Reich-Sachs-Galbraith et al), the JVP-NPP Govt would know that the economic strategy and model it is determinedly following will only further polarisation, deepen the affordability crisis, and is doomed to fail.

Clearly, the ruling JVP-NPP rather than Sajith’s SJB or Namal’s SLPP, has become the main agency of neoliberal economic doctrine, strategy and policy in Sri Lanka.

Harsha’s hype

Dr Harsha de Silva’s argument is that economic stabilisation has been positive and successful, the NPP Government’s ‘reform agenda’ and ‘direction’ are laudable, but insufficient because growth is now needed. The NPP comfortably concurs, calling it ‘transformation’. His critique of the Government’s economics is tactical and managerial: ignorance and incompetence in implementation.

Harsha adds an absurdity: the lingering Marxism-Leninism of the JVP foredooms it to failure at generating rapid, sustainable growth in a market economy. He should identify and prove the existence of the ‘Marxist-Leninist’ component instead of taking Handunetti’s word for it. (Sunil should know it isn’t meant to be ‘lodged in the heart’, but the head.) Harsha clearly doesn’t agree with Sajith that the JVP has betrayed Marxism/socialism and converted to neoliberalism.

Harsha’s contention on Marxism-Leninism and economics is vaporised by the achievement of the Communist Parties of China and Vietnam. His position is different from Sajith’s contestable yet understandable declaration that China and Vietnam’s economies are capitalist. (I’d say they are better understood as ‘hybrid systems’ or a ‘systemic fusion’.) Sajith wisely never contradicts the fact that the foundations and core convictions of the Chinese and Vietnamese CPs are Marxist-Leninist.

Harsha de Silva should read Kevin Rudd or Shiran Illanperuma on China, to comprehend whether Marxism-Leninism is an intrinsic obstacle to an economic miracle, let alone sustainable rapid growth—or is a very real part of the mix in China. But then again, Harsha the economist never mentions the Chinese economic miracle, unprecedented in economic history.

Harsha doesn’t get the JVP-NPP’s dark dualism: ultra-capitalist economics, one-party (‘Marxist-Leninist’) political rule.

‘Poor made poorer, rich made richer’

Sajith’s Budget speech was a masterclass; intellectually, substantively, the best on both sides of the aisle. (https://youtu.be/T_Ss7xsvxrQ?si=FrsjJmNKfUYGQYnw)

He refused to give AKD – and Ranil Wickremesinghe—a free pass on ‘economic stabilisation’. Instead, he de-constructed the ‘economic stabilisation’ itself:

“…Therefore, indeed, when you claim conditions have normalised, I wish to state that normalisation has occurred to the advantage of multi-trillionaires and the ultra-rich—to the disadvantage of the poor, the common public, the working class, and the middle class…”

(https://www.dailymirror.lk/news-features/Government-has-betrayed-people-by-embracing-neoliberal-policies/131-354920)

The Daily FT report of his speech prefaces the text with key takeaways as bullet-points:

Says poorest 20%’s real household income fell 19.6% in 2019-2025, richest 20%’s rose 6.8%

Claims only $ 1 b FDI came in 2025 as several projects exited

Says Lazard gave SL worse debt deal than Ghana and Senegal

Only 5 of 17 IT sector pledges for 2026 delivered, he says

Urges vehicle permits for professionals to stem brain drain

(https://www.ft.lk/front-page/Sajith-brands-Budget-2027-a-string-of-lies/44-800098)

‘…Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa yesterday…charged that the 2027 Budget widens inequality, fails to draw foreign investment and offers no relief to farmers, small businesses or public servants.

…Premadasa said income had shifted from the poor to the rich between 2019 and 2025. Real household income of the poorest 20% fell by 19.6%, while that of the richest 20% rose by 6.8%, he said, widening the average income gap between the two groups from 11.2 times to 14.8 times. He said the richest 20%’s share of income had risen to 55.8%, which he blamed on inadequate wages, soaring inflation and the erosion of living support. He tabled the survey in Hansard.

“The poor were made poorer, and the rich were made richer,” he said.

… The Government had failed to change the debt sustainability analysis (DSA) agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), as promised in its manifesto “A Thriving Nation – A Beautiful Life”. He said Lazard, the firm that brokered the deal with international sovereign bondholders, had also handled restructurings for Ghana and Senegal, which secured better terms.

He took issue with the macro-linked Bonds in the deal, under which debt relief shrinks as economic growth rises.

“Then what incentive or motivation do we have as a country to increase the economic growth rate? As the growth rate rises, the amount of foreign debt we have to repay also increases. Lazard defrauded Sri Lanka,” he said.

He said there had been no debt restructuring for the 263,000 micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in distress in 2022, a number he said had since grown. The promised development bank for them had not been set up. The Government had suspended the parate law, which lets banks auction pledged property without going to court, but had not restructured MSME debt, he said.

…He said farmers were promised Rs. 150 per kg of paddy, but prices had fallen to a maximum of Rs. 95. He said the promised interest-free loans and price support through small and medium millers had not materialised, and that cultivation of big onions, potatoes, chillies, upland crops, fruit, export crops and upcountry vegetables had collapsed.

“You have not provided even an atom of support for agriculture through this Budget,” he said.

Premadasa accused the Government of spending hundreds of billions of rupees of public money on thermal power at the expense of renewable energy…and said the promised LNG had not materialised. He challenged the Government to name a single production industry it had initiated.

He said a World Bank report of October 2026 found that 60% of the country was poor, while the UNDP Multidimensional Poverty Report showed poverty had escalated severely. He said the Government and the Department of Census and Statistics wrongly used a blanket average of 2,030 kilocalories per person per day, when the Medical Research Institute showed needs vary by gender and activity. This error led to the claim that Rs. 17,742 a month was enough for one person, he said.

…He asked why the 15% interest on savings promised to senior citizens had not been granted, and said retirees’ core problems remained unresolved.

Premadasa said the Budget had no proposal for the promised 33% cut in electricity bills, and that pledges of a Rs. 1.2 million Vitz car, a Rs. 50,000 motorcycle and fuel at port landing prices had not been kept.

He said schools could not secure smart boards or computers, and the health sector faced severe shortages of drugs, equipment and staff. He asked what had happened to the promised fish-locating app and the plan to develop marine resources in the 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone. To stem the brain, drain, he urged the Government to grant vehicle permits to professionals, including doctors, rather than to MPs.

Premadasa…described it [the Budget] as one that “strikes the stomach of the common man and the poor”.

He urged the Government to reject neo-liberalism and extreme Marxism and adopt “the middle path, social democracy, and the social market economy”.’ (https://www.ft.lk/front-page/Sajith-brands-Budget-2027-a-string-of-lies/44-800098)

Socio-economic model

The statistics and diagrams that Sajith tabled reveal that the seismic shift of real income from the poor and working people to the very rich began in 2019. This establishes the truth: the model which enables the unprecedented dominance of “the multi-trillionaires, the ultra-rich”; the tectonic shift in policy paradigm, began with Gotabaya Rajapaksa, ran through Gota’s choice (unelected) Ranil Wickremesinghe, and reached the next level with Anura Dissanayake.

I was there with Sanja, seated behind Mahinda Rajapaksa, when it happened in May 2018 at the Viyath Maga 2nd Convention at the Hotel Shangri-la. The top corporate owners and head-honchos were all present. As I noted at the time:

‘…we were able to see the heaviest hitters of Colombo’s corporate class…Ken Balendra, Harry Jayawardena, and Merrill Fernando among them. The heavy hitters weren’t lurking on the flanks, hedging their bets. They didn’t mind being up front, literally and metaphorically. The bourgeoisie had just defected from a UNP Government.’

(https://www.colombotelegraph.com/index.php/gotabayas-operation-shangri-la/)

The content of the proceedings constituted an ideological-policy coup, displacing Mahinda’s policies. The line and line-up of the inaugural Viyath Maga Convention at Golden Rose Battaramulla March 2017, was replaced. I recall MR over the phone the next morning expressing incredulity and horrified disagreement with the ideas aired by the speakers (except Nalaka Godahewa) the previous evening. Two years later, MR’s powers as PM were removed and vested in the President through the 20th amendment, by those who came into office riding on his shoulders. Two years after that, they were overthrown by the Aragalaya (2022).

I  called it, in the Daily Mirror, 22 May 2018:

‘…The GR model as unveiled at Viyath Maga gave no importance to poverty, the peasantry, landlessness, inequity, poverty reduction, and social upliftment. It had no place for the people or social justice. The goal was high economic growth with law and order. Social questions and public welfare were conspicuously absent and the assumption seemed to be ‘trickle down’. The vision is socially ‘thin’, ungrounded; a holographic projection with little social ‘thickness’, inclusivity, depth or rootedness in complex social reality…’

(Re-posted in https://www.lankaweb.com/news/items/2018/05/22/gotabayas-breakthrough/)

I proceeded to predict contradictions that would be generated along three axial routes, which subsequently materialised, triggering the Aragalaya:

(I)‘The South-South axis, where social insensitivity, inequity and structural marginalisation will trigger clashes with students, workers, peasants, fisherfolk and neighbourhood communities.

(II)The North-South axis, where tokenistic integrationism/assimilationism in place of a geopolitically sustainable political equation, will render the Tamil Question utterly intractable.

(III)The Democracy-Autocracy axis, where the top-down technocratic model itself requires authoritarianism …and will thereby erode legitimacy and trigger resistance…’                   (Daily Mirror, 22 May, 2018)

At Viyath Maga-2 (2018), the ultra-rich shifted from Ranil’s UNP to Gotabaya. When the Aragalaya ousted Gota, they shifted back to his nominee Ranil. From Ranil they transitioned to Anura and obtained the greatest and most direct policy influence since Independence.

The three contradictions I projected in May 2018 have begun to manifest themselves and characterise AKD-JVP-NPP rule too, proving the continuity of the model.

The pivot

Sajith Premadasa’s deconstruction of the 2027 Budget and the AKD administration’s trajectory since 2024 (preceded by Ranil Wickremesinghe’s), is the first ideological and doctrinal departure in the democratic political mainstream from the hegemonic elite consensus dating from 2018, and the first pivot to a social democratic centrism.

Sajith’s Budget speech (belatedly) approximates the advice given to him (on camera, reported in the media) by the finest Finance Minister we had, Ronnie de Mel, when Sajith and Harsha paid a call on his 91st birthday: “[to revive the Open Economy] bring the whole thing under the control of the ideas you hold, and infuse it with a strong dose of socialist values.”

This year Sajith explicitly critiqued neoliberal right-wing economics and asserted the imperative of ‘Middle Path-Social Democracy-Social Market Economy’ to an audience of Opposition (not merely SJB) politicians at a Pre-Budget Workshop in Colombo. (https://youtu.be/4u_NNpIrCj4?si=l6sxaaIELwR-EoLn)

title: $ 500 m epic gambit: Can Ramayana globalise Indian cinema and redefine its most ancient story? | Daily FT

Few cultural narratives carry the weight, reverence, and antiquity of the Ramayana. For millennia, this monumental Sanskrit epic has shaped the moral, philosophical, and artistic landscape of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Yet, the recent cinematic adaptation of this ancient saga represents a bold departure from traditional mythological storytelling. Conceived as a quintessential Indian enterprise—featuring an all-Indian cast, director, and production team—the film takes one of India's oldest stories and reimagines it through the visual language of modern event cinema. By opting for a high-concept, visual-effects-driven treatment reminiscent of Hollywood blockbusters like Avatar, the filmmakers have aligned the epic with a VFX-heavy sci-fi/fantasy genre that currently dominates Western multiplexes. Industry insiders and international trade analysts have described the project as a staggering $ 500 million gambit: a calculated, ambitious attempt to breach the global mainstream and firmly establish Indian cinema on the world stage.

Early box office signals and the global footprint

Initial five-day box office reports indicate that this massive financial gamble is generating significant early returns. The film has recorded remarkable ticket sales across a broad geographic footprint, taking in strong numbers not only in domestic Indian centers but also throughout North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and Southeast Asia.

Most notably, trade data indicates that roughly 37% of the film’s total initial revenue was generated outside India. For an Indian production, achieving such a substantial share of total revenue from foreign markets within the opening week is historically unprecedented. It marks a clear milestone in the international distribution of South Asian cinema, demonstrating that an Indian narrative can generate substantial box office activity simultaneously across multiple continents.

Several distinct factors have converged to drive this foreign performance:

Comparative realities: Overseas diaspora vs. genuine crossover

Despite these impressive early figures, a deeper analytical look reveals a more nuanced commercial picture. When evaluated strictly against global Hollywood behemoths such as Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer or other recent tentpole releases, the film’s initial five-day international revenue remains noticeably lower. Declaring the project a complete global crossover success requires qualification.

The film faced structural hurdles in Western markets, including screen allocations in North America that were significantly smaller than those granted to major studio releases. Furthermore, demographic tracking shows that the vast majority of foreign ticket sales were driven by the South Asian diaspora rather than a broad, non-Indian mainstream audience.

Consequently, while the film represents a pioneering foray into foreign markets, its ultimate profitability remains anchored to domestic box office performance in India. Nevertheless, this ambitious release model provides vital data and strategic lessons for future Indian productions aiming for international crossover appeal.

The Ravana paradigm: Humanising the antagonist

Beyond its commercial trajectory, the film has sparked intense debate over its narrative choices and characterisation—most prominently in its portrayal of Ravana, the primary antagonist of the epic.

Traditionally depicted as a ten-headed demon king symbolising moral failing and hubris, Ravana is presented in this adaptation as a deeply nuanced figure: a scholar of extraordinary intellect, a formidable warrior, a master of arts and sciences, and a ruler of vast capacity. This complex portrayal gives the character dramatic weight that rivaled—and in the eyes of many viewers, overshadowed—the heroic arc of Ram.

The strength of this performance sparked widespread discourse across social media, with one prominent digital influencer cheekily dubbing the release “Ravana Leela” to highlight how thoroughly the antagonist commands the screen. By reframing Ravana through a lens of tragic grandeur and intellectual mastery, the film has reopened long-standing discussions around villainy, nuance, and character perspective within ancient Indian literature.

History, myth, and geographical debates

The film’s release has also reignited the debate surrounding the historical validity of the epic itself, dividing audiences into distinct interpretive camps:

1. The mythological viewpoint: Sceptics and academic traditionalists maintain that the Ramayana should be classified primarily as literature and mythology, pointing to a lack of empirical, standardised archaeological evidence confirming the specific supernatural and historical events described in the text.

2.The historical viewpoint: Believers argue that the narrative is rooted in actual historical events preserved through a continuous oral tradition. Proponents frequently cite regional geography, ancient cultural traditions, and ongoing archaeological research across India and Sri Lanka as indicators of a real historical core.

Compounding this debate is the question of ancient geography—specifically, whether the "Lanka" described in Valmiki’s original text corresponds to the modern island nation of Sri Lanka. While popular belief firmly equates the two, some historical geographers and scholars suggest that the ancient Lanka may have been located in central or northern India. Conversely, in Sri Lanka, the film's dignified presentation of Ravana has been met with enthusiasm among local cultural groups who revere the ancient king as a heroic figure of native heritage and ancient sovereignty.

Strategic opportunities and the path ahead

Irrespective of its final box office totals, this cinematic adaptation presents tangible strategic opportunities across multiple sectors:

For the Indian film industry

The production serves as a proof of concept for global distribution strategies. Filmmakers can analyse its performance metrics, localisation techniques (such as AI dubbing), and international co-productions to refine how Indian stories are packaged and marketed for foreign markets.

For Sri Lankan cultural tourism

The heightened interest in Ravana offers Sri Lanka a unique opportunity to expand its heritage tourism. The island possesses numerous sites traditionally associated with the epic, ranging from ancient caves to mountain fortresses. As explored in Sunela Jayawardene’s book Ravana’s Lanka, rich oral traditions and folklore point to an ancient Yaksha civilisation pre-dating later historical migrations. By systematically developing and promoting a "Ravana Trail," Sri Lanka could attract history enthusiasts, pilgrims, and travelers from across the Indian subcontinent and beyond.

Key questions for the future of Indian epic cinema

Will India's oldest epic ultimately serve as the vanguard that breaks down international barriers, establishing a sustainable template to attract non-Indian viewers to South Asian cinema?

 Will global and domestic audiences permanently adopt a more nuanced view of Ravana, moving away from a traditional archetype toward a recognition of his scholarly intellect and tragic complexity?

 Will Sri Lanka capitalise on this cultural interest by leveraging the legacy of Ravana to build a thriving cultural tourism sector around its ancient heritage?

title: Greater tax powers need greater taxpayer safeguards | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 19 November 2026 03:56
-     - 48

Budget 2027 has made a welcome start in fixing the fine print of tax administration. But as the Commissioner General is equipped with stronger enforcement tools, taxpayers need an equally strong safeguard when the system gets it wrong. An independent Tax Ombudsman should be the next step, not an afterthought. Fair taxes require fair process. And fair process requires somewhere for the taxpayer to turn

When a Budget is read, the headlines naturally go to the big numbers: a higher tax-free threshold, wider tax slabs, a levy abolished or a tariff cut. These measures grab attention because people feel them directly in their pay packets and shopping baskets.

Yet some of the more consequential proposals in Budget 2027 are tucked away in the annexures, expressed in the technical language of section numbers and procedure. They may not trend on social media, but they shape the day-to-day relationship between the taxpayer and the tax administration.

One passage in the Budget Speech is particularly important. Under “Strengthening Tax Administration and Facilitating Taxpayer Compliance”, the Government acknowledges that stringent procedural requirements can result in taxpayers being denied legitimate refunds or input tax credits because of technical or procedural non-compliance. It proposes to remove ambiguities, accommodate evolving business practices and create what it describes as a “fair, transparent, and efficient tax administration system”.

That is an important acknowledgement. Tax administration should protect Government revenue, but it should also protect taxpayers’ legitimate entitlements.

When procedure defeats substance

For years, tax practitioners have encountered the same problem. A business may have incurred VAT on a genuine transaction and hold the necessary supporting documentation, yet lose its input tax credit because a statutory timeline was interpreted narrowly. The transaction is real and the tax has been incurred, but a procedural failure can result in the credit being lost.

That sits uneasily with the fundamental design of VAT as a tax on value addition. When legitimate input credits are denied purely on technical grounds, VAT can begin to operate more like a cascading tax, increasing the effective tax cost through the supply chain.

Budget 2027 responds with several targeted amendments. Input tax will be claimable within a uniform 12-month period for local purchases and 24 months for imports, irrespective of the date on which the VAT return is submitted. Importantly, this separates the substantive entitlement to claim from the timing of the return.

The Budget also addresses a legacy issue from the pandemic. Input tax claims previously disallowed because VAT returns were delayed during the COVID-19 period may be claimed by eligible taxpayers, provided the outstanding returns were filed by 31 July 2026.

This is a welcome correction. Businesses that operated through exceptional pandemic-related disruptions should not continue to bear a tax cost merely because procedural requirements could not be met on time.

When the two languages of the law disagree

Another proposed amendment illustrates how basic some tax administration problems can be.

The Government intends to correct discrepancies between the Sinhala and English texts of the VAT provisions governing input tax claims. A difference between two statutory texts is more than a drafting inconvenience. It creates uncertainty over taxpayers’ rights and obligations, leaves room for competing interpretations and ultimately increases the cost of compliance and dispute resolution.

Other longstanding areas of uncertainty are also being addressed. The treatment of credit and debit notes will be aligned with the timing of input tax claims, including adjustments in circumstances where tax invoices have not been issued.

The VAT treatment of Non-Foreign Exchange (NFE) transactions, non-tax invoices and the consequential effects of exemptions will also be clarified. Each amendment may look minor in isolation. Collectively, however, they remove grey areas that have generated queries, assessments and appeals.

Certainty for cross-border transactions

The Inland Revenue Act will similarly receive a series of clarifications.

Section 85(1B) will be amended to clarify that the 14% withholding tax on service fees and insurance premiums applies to payments made to non-residents without a permanent establishment in Sri Lanka. This should address uncertainty surrounding payments to non-residents that are already within the Sri Lankan tax net through a permanent establishment. The applicable rate would, of course, remain subject to any relief available under a relevant Double Taxation Agreement.

Section 73 will also be amended so that income from remote and digital services, including online advertising and cloud services, is sourced by reference to the place of payment.

Section 75(5) will be updated by replacing the reference to the “prevention of fiscal evasion” with the “prevention of tax evasion and avoidance”. The amendment aligns the terminology with the OECD and UN Model Double Taxation Conventions and reflects the broader international focus on addressing both tax evasion and abusive tax avoidance.

Confidentiality safeguards will also be tightened so that information received from foreign tax authorities is disclosed only to authorised persons and, where required, with the prior consent of the relevant foreign tax authority. Such safeguards are essential if Sri Lanka is to remain a trusted partner in international tax information exchange.

Anti-avoidance needs certainty too

Not all of the administrative changes are about taxpayer relief.

New anti-avoidance rules are proposed to address tax avoidance through company amalgamations and mergers, while seeking to ensure that genuine amalgamations are not unduly affected. That proviso matters. Anti-avoidance rules are legitimate and necessary tools for protecting the revenue base. But if drafted too broadly, they can also capture commercially sound restructurings. The concept of a “genuine” amalgamation therefore requires clarity. The legislation should spell out both the circumstances in which the anti-avoidance rule will apply and the resulting tax consequences of an amalgamation.

Ultimately, the success of this proposal will depend not only on its objective, but on the precision of the drafting and the consistency with which it is administered.

Other administration-related provisions 

Other practical measures are also welcome. The Commissioner General of Inland Revenue will accept a certificate from an approved accountant, or such other authorised person as may be specified, to verify a taxpayer's compliance with the existing statutory restrictions on cash transactions. This brings professionals more directly into the compliance process.

If approved accountants or other authorised persons are expected to provide such certification, however, the law should clearly define the scope of their verification obligations, responsibility and liability. Professional certification should not become an open-ended assumption of responsibility where the boundaries of what the certifier is required to verify are unclear.

Provisions will also be introduced to prevent the double taxation of donations passed between NGOs, subject to the submission of proof confirming that the tax was paid by the original recipient NGO. This is another sensible correction.

Taken together, these may appear to be technical amendments. But they share an important objective: greater certainty about what the law requires and how it will be administered.

Stronger administration must mean stronger safeguards

This brings us to the more fundamental issue.

Budget 2027 deserves credit for addressing administrative problems that rarely attract political attention. Clearer legislation, more workable procedures and the correction of technical anomalies can materially improve the taxpayer experience.

But clearer laws do not eliminate disputes. Nor do they eliminate administrative discretion. Assessments will still be raised. Refunds will still be delayed. Administrative powers may occasionally be applied inconsistently or disproportionately.

That matters even more today because the powers available to the Commissioner General of Inland Revenue have expanded. The previous amendment to the Inland Revenue Act introduced criminal sanctions for specified compliance failures, strengthening the enforcement tools available to the tax administration.

Stronger enforcement may well be necessary to improve compliance. But greater powers should be accompanied by greater accountability and equally robust safeguards for taxpayers.

Challenging an administrative decision through the formal objection and appeal process is not equally accessible to all taxpayers, given the cost and time involved. For individual taxpayers and small and medium-sized enterprises in particular, the burden can be significant. A delayed refund is not merely an administrative inconvenience; it can become a cash-flow problem and, at times, a threat to survival. For many, prolonged appeals may simply be beyond practical reach.

The question, therefore, is not whether the revenue authority should have the powers necessary to administer and enforce the tax law. It should. The question is: when those powers are misapplied, exercised inconsistently or used disproportionately, where can the ordinary taxpayer turn?

The Tax Ombudsman: The clear missing piece

This is where Budget 2027 could have gone further.

An independent Tax Ombudsman would provide an accessible and impartial avenue for taxpayers to raise administrative grievances without immediately entering the formal appeals or court process.

Its role would not be to undermine the Commissioner General, interfere with legitimate tax collection or replace the statutory appeal mechanism. Rather, it would address the space between taxpayer service and formal litigation such as unreasonable delays, procedural failures, inconsistent treatment, difficulties in obtaining refunds, failures to respond, and instances where administrative powers appear to have been exercised unfairly or disproportionately.

The Budget Speech itself makes the case. It speaks of safeguarding “the taxpayers’ legitimate entitlements” and establishing a “fair, transparent, and efficient tax administration system”. Entitlements written into law mean little unless there is a practical, affordable way to enforce them.

If enforcement powers are strengthened on one side, the institutional mechanisms protecting taxpayers must evolve on the other. This is why the absence of a Tax Ombudsman is clearly missed opportunity in Budget 2027.

Trust is built in the fine print

Voluntary compliance does not come from enforcement alone. It grows when taxpayers believe the system is predictable, consistent and fair.

Every legitimate credit denied, every refund unnecessarily delayed and every uncertainty left unresolved weakens that confidence. Every ambiguity removed, every procedure made more workable and every genuine entitlement protected strengthens it.

Budget 2027 has made a welcome start in fixing the fine print of tax administration. But as the Commissioner General is equipped with stronger enforcement tools, taxpayers need an equally strong safeguard when the system gets it wrong. An independent Tax Ombudsman should be the next step, not an afterthought. Fair taxes require fair process. And fair process requires somewhere for the taxpayer to turn.

(The views expressed in this article are those of the author in her personal capacity)

title: Budget 2027: Can Sri Lanka turn ambition into growth? | Daily FT

Sri Lanka’s 2027 Budget, presented by the President on 12 November 2026, is an important test of the country’s economic recovery. It comes at a critical juncture: the current IMF program is due to conclude in March 2027, debt remains a major constraint, and the economy must move from stabilisation towards sustainable, investment-led growth.

The Budget has several positive features. It recognises the need to increase capital investment, strengthen revenue administration, support SMEs, improve infrastructure and accelerate digital transformation. The proposed public investment of approximately Rs. 2 trillion, equivalent to 5.12% of GDP, including the supplementary allocation for Cyclone Ditwah recovery, is significant. However, the real test will not be the size of the allocation, but how much is translated into productive investment.

Sri Lanka has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to announce ambitious budgets. Its more persistent weakness has been implementation.

The financing challenge

The Government’s gross borrowing requirement of Rs. 3.8 trillion raises important questions about financing sustainability. With no International Sovereign Bond issuance explicitly indicated in the 2027 borrowing plan, the extent to which domestic financial institutions will be required to finance Government borrowing deserves scrutiny. Excessive reliance on domestic borrowing could crowd out private-sector credit and increase the banking system’s exposure to sovereign debt.

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake making his way along the Parliament corridors on 12 November on his way to deliver the 2027 Budget Speech

The debt-service burden

Approximately Rs. 4,850 billion is required for debt servicing, equivalent to nearly 79% of projected Government revenue of approximately Rs. 6.15 trillion. With foreign debt-service obligations expected to rise further in 2028, the Government must demonstrate how it intends to build adequate foreign-exchange buffers.

The conclusion of the current IMF program also requires clarity on the way forward beyond 2027. The Government has appointed a committee to examine the suitability and nature of a successor arrangement. Sri Lanka needs to make this decision early. Fiscal credibility, access to external financing and investor confidence cannot be left to uncertainty.

Tax relief and revenue mobilisation

The Budget’s tax proposals provide some relief. Increasing the personal income tax-free threshold to Rs. 162,500 per month will benefit salaried employees, while reducing CESS rates on 800 selected Harmonised System (HS) code lines by 25% could lower trade costs and improve competitiveness.

However, these tax concessions are estimated to result in a net annual revenue loss of approximately Rs. 28.4 billion. The Government must balance relief measures with revenue mobilisation and ensure that these concessions do not compromise its revenue targets.

Closing the capital expenditure execution gap

The most important question is whether the Government can execute its ambitious capital program. Historical performance shows that only 64% of the capital budget was utilised in 2023, 54% in 2024 and 76% in 2025. Increasing allocations without addressing procurement delays, fragmented approvals, weak project management and shortages of technical expertise will not deliver the desired economic returns.

The Government must move towards a project-based accountability system. Every major investment should have a clearly identified project owner, measurable milestones, a realistic cash-flow plan and quarterly progress reporting. Projects should be assessed for economic viability and implementation readiness before funds are allocated.

Equally important is the capacity of the public service to deliver. The Government must attract and retain the engineers, procurement specialists and project managers required to implement an investment program of this scale. Budget allocations must translate into completed infrastructure rather than remain unspent provisions.

Unlocking private investment

Public investment alone cannot deliver the growth Sri Lanka needs. The country must attract domestic and foreign private capital, particularly into infrastructure, energy, tourism, logistics, manufacturing and technology. The proposed public-private partnership framework and reforms to State-owned enterprises are therefore important.

The Government’s medium-term ambition of achieving sustainable economic growth of 7% or higher will require a more competitive investment environment, predictable policies, faster approvals and stronger investor protection. The challenge is how quickly the Government can translate its ambitions into an investable project pipeline capable of attracting domestic and foreign investors.

The proposed SME financing programs are welcome, but credit schemes must be supported by appropriate risk-sharing arrangements, sound lending criteria and transparent reporting of repayment performance. Ultimately, sustainable SME growth must come from improving productivity, market access and competitiveness rather than relying solely on subsidised credit.

Technology, AI and automation

Digital transformation offers an opportunity to improve tax collection, public procurement and service delivery. Investment in revenue administration systems is particularly important if Sri Lanka is to broaden its tax base and improve compliance. Digital project tracking, e-procurement and AI-based analytics could also help identify implementation delays, reduce inefficiencies and strengthen public accountability.

However, technology investment must be accompanied by investment in people. Government officers need the digital, analytical and AI competencies to use these systems effectively. Cybersecurity and the protection of citizens’ personal data are equally important.

Parliament, business chambers and citizens should also have access to regular progress reports showing how Budget proposals are being implemented, how much has been spent and what outcomes have been achieved.

Turning ambition into results

Sri Lanka has made considerable progress in restoring macroeconomic stability. The next phase must focus on productivity, exports and sustainability, alongside infrastructure upgrading, investment and employment creation. The Government must also ensure that the burden of economic recovery does not fall disproportionately on the private sector and ordinary citizens.

Budget 2027 has the potential to become a turning point. But potential is not performance. The real measure of success will be whether the Government can convert its plans into working projects, its allocations into productive assets and its reforms into sustainable economic opportunities.

Ultimately, the Government’s challenge is not only to grow revenue through taxes and fees and strengthen public finances, but also to grow the economy, create productive employment and improve the livelihoods of ordinary people, thereby reducing poverty. Fiscal discipline must be a means to an end, not an end in itself.

The true measure of Budget 2027 will be whether economic growth translates into better incomes, greater opportunities and a higher quality of life for all Sri Lankans.
